conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Take your time. The team will support you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I feel more prepared now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here to help. A nurse will come by with your prescriptions and wound care instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get everything arranged. Rest, stay on top of your meds, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Ms. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you were brought in after your caregiver found you with low blood sugar and some shaking movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was feeling weak and then my arms started jerking. I couldn’t control it. My sugar was really low, but it came up after they gave me juice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Low sugar can cause twitching, but since it’s still happening, we need to look into other causes. We’ve checked your labs and found your sodium is low, and you have an infection marker slightly elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sodium? I didn’t know that could affect me like this. Is that why I’m twitching?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be part of it, especially since you're on dialysis. But we also think one of your antibiotics—Ciprofloxacin—could be causing these jerks. It’s known to do that in some patients, especially with kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve been on that since my last hospital stay for the foot infection. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already stopped it. We’re switching you to an IV antibiotic called Ceftazidime, which is safer for you and still treats the bone infection in your heel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. But my leg still hurts a lot. Is the infection getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infection is still there, and we’re treating it aggressively. But the teams—podiatry, vascular, and infectious disease—still believe a below-the-knee amputation is the best long-term solution to heal you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know they’ve said that before. I just need more time to think. I’m not ready for surgery yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. You don’t have to decide now. But we want you to know it’s not just about infection—it’s also about your dialysis access. The transplant team says they can’t place a new graft until the infection is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t get a better dialysis line until my leg is taken care of?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s all connected. We’re not pushing, but we want you to have all the information when you talk to the surgeons again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs improved overnight. Your sodium went up to 132 after your dialysis session, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And the jerking? I haven’t noticed it since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. We think stopping the Cipro helped. We’ll keep monitoring, but it looks like the myoclonus is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was really scared something was wrong with my brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your neurology—your reflexes and mental status are intact. No signs of stroke or seizure. This was likely a medication and metabolic issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but okay. My leg is still sore, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given your IV antibiotic after dialysis, as planned. The infection markers are coming down, but the wound is still concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the urine test? I remember they said something about bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine had mixed bacteria, but it looks like contamination. No active UTI, so we’re not treating it. But we still recommend straight catheterization every other day to prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nurse does that at home. I have a urology appointment coming up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, next week. They’ll help decide if you need a long-term catheter or other options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed everything with the team. Your twitching is gone, sodium is stable, and infection signs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. You’ll continue IV antibiotics during dialysis and keep taking Flagyl at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I was on 30 units, but you changed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We lowered it to 25 units because your sugars were running low. You can go back to 30 if they stay stable, but we’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And Gabapentin? I’ve been on it for years for nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused it at first because it can rarely cause jerking, but since your symptoms improved without restarting it, we’ll let you resume at home unless you notice any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart medicine? I’m not on blood thinners anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We stopped warfarin due to concerns about calciphylaxis, but dermatology said it’s unlikely. With your high stroke risk, your primary team should re-evaluate restarting a blood thinner soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask my doctor. I don’t want to have a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your labs are stable, no more twitching, and you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue IV antibiotics at dialysis, take Flagyl three times a day, and keep your insulin as prescribed. The visiting nurse will catheterize you every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leg? When do I see the surgeons?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a call from podiatry and vascular surgery within the week. They’ll help you decide about the amputation. We know it’s a big decision, but it’s the best chance for healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Call us if your weight goes up more than three pounds, or if you have fever, pain, or confusion. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in because your blood sugar was over 500. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay, just tired. My foot’s been bothering me, and my sugars have been really hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You’ve been on antibiotics for your foot infection—vancomycin and ceftazidime. We think the infection might be making your sugars worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this ulcer for so long. Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still concerning. You’re scheduled for a below-the-knee amputation next week to help control the infection. We discussed it with vascular surgery, and they’re still planning to go ahead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’m nervous about the surgery. Will I be safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your heart and overall health. You’re at higher risk because of your heart and diabetes, but we’ll make sure you’re ready. You may need to see cardiology before the surgery for clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered changing them because of resistant bacteria we’ve seen in the past, but you’re not showing signs of being very sick. We briefly switched to cefepime, but we’re going back to your usual vancomycin and ceftazidime since you want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stay in the hospital longer. I can take them at dialysis, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You’ll get vancomycin and ceftazidime after each dialysis session, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood sugar—what’s going on there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for diabetic ketoacidosis, but your blood isn’t acidic, so it’s not DKA. The infection is likely spiking your sugars. We gave you insulin, and it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my sliding scale. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep your usual insulin—NPH in the morning and the sliding scale as needed. We’ll keep an eye on it while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve also been feeling a bit short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. There’s some fluid buildup in your lungs from heart failure. You’re scheduled for dialysis today to help remove extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot I had that today. Will it help me breathe better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most patients feel better after dialysis. We’ll also keep you on your heart meds—lisinopril, carvedilol, and others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my sodium was low last time. Is that still an issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium was 132 when you came in, but it’s now 136—much better. Nephrology recommends you stay on a 1-liter fluid restriction daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s hard not to drink more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Just do your best. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but my breathing feels easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your blood pressure is better too—131/50. The fluid removal helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any other test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is normal, so no major infection right now. The urine test showed some bacteria, but it’s likely contamination. No treatment change needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many UTIs. I’m not surprised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your history of catheter use, you’re at high risk. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar this morning is 140—well controlled. How’s your foot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still sore, but no new drainage or redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The wound looks stable. We’re keeping the dressing clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about gabapentin? I’ve been taking it for nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned you didn’t want to continue it. We’ve stopped it, and you can restart if needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m okay without it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. We’re getting close to discharge. Your labs are stable—sodium 136, glucose 119, and hemoglobin improved to 11.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Am I going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home with services to help you until surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my surgery prep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve told vascular surgery you’re high risk. They recommend you see cardiology before the amputation for clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make that appointment. And I keep my fluid limit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1 liter per day. Also, weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. You’ll keep all your usual meds except gabapentin, which we stopped. Insulin, antibiotics with dialysis, heart meds—all continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re doing well—alert, breathing fine, sugars controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: follow up with your primary doctor, keep your clinic appointments, and good luck with surgery next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a note to your podiatrist and vascular surgeon to keep them updated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I want everyone on the same page.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re all working together for your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—call us if your foot gets red, warm, or starts draining, or if your sugars go over 300 consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if it’s worse than usual. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well this admission. We’re confident you’ll do well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and good luck next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need it!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve got a strong team behind you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up or hear how the surgery went.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , part of the surgery team. You're here for cardiac optimization before your planned left below-the-knee amputation, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My foot ulcer hasn’t healed, and they said it’s time. I’m nervous about the surgery and my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’re going to make sure your heart is stable before the surgery. We’ll do a stress test and work closely with cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues before—CHF, AFib, and a bypass. Will that make the surgery riskier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those do increase risk, which is why we’re taking this step of cardiac optimization. We want to reduce any complications during or after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What tests will I have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a P-MIBI stress test to check for heart ischemia. We’ll also do a chest X-ray today to check your lungs and heart size.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis? I’m on it three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue your regular hemodialysis schedule. We’ve scheduled sessions before surgery to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I remember last time I was bloated and short of breath when I missed one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keeping your fluid status stable helps your heart and makes surgery safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back. It shows mild cardiomegaly and a little fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia or collapse. Your central line is in good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The fluid in my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild, and we expect it given your heart failure. Dialysis will help remove the extra fluid. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stress test was completed. Good news—no signs of cardiac ischemia. Cardiology cleared you for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief! When will the surgery be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll do dialysis today to optimize your volume status before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood sugars? They’ve been hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HbA1c was 8.2, which is elevated. We’ll manage your insulin carefully during your stay to keep sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my antibiotics? I’ve been on vancomycin and ceftazidime at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued both for surgical prophylaxis. You’ll keep them with each dialysis session after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. My legs feel less heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That means the fluid removal is helping. Rest well tonight. Surgery is at 8 a.m. tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Ms. ___. You made it through the surgery. You had a left below-the-knee amputation, and it went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My leg… it’s gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the lower part of your left leg was removed. The wound is closed with staples. We placed nerve catheters for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have a lot of pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing it well. The nerve catheters are helping. You’ll also get oral Dilaudid as needed. We’ll switch to a fentanyl patch soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nerve catheters were removed this afternoon. How’s your pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still sore, but the pills help. The patch is on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the fentanyl patch is in place. It will help with ongoing limb pain. Your PCP will help wean it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed a small amount of redness around your incision. It’s mild cellulitis, so we’re continuing vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Could it get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and caught early. With antibiotics, it should resolve. We’ll keep a close eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t urinated much. I’ve had this problem before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your chart notes urinary retention. We catheterized you and got 350cc. We’ll monitor and avoid a Foley if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your incision is clean, and the redness is improving. Physical therapy saw you and recommends rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rehab? I’ll need help learning to move?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to build strength, prevent knee contractures, and prepare for a prosthesis. You’ll go to an extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood thinners? I was on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your history of HIT and calciphylaxis, we started apixaban instead. You’ll take it twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe after surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We held one dose when removing the nerve catheters. Now that healing is underway, it’s safe to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back with yeast. It’s likely related to your history of urogenital candidiasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re not symptomatic, and it’s likely colonization. We’ll watch for symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your incision is healing well. The mild cellulitis is resolving. We’ll keep the antibiotics for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fentanyl patch? I’m worried about being on strong pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wean it slowly after discharge. Your PCP will help manage that to avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology updated your meds: atorvastatin 80 mg daily and lisinopril increased to 20 mg. Imdur and hydralazine are stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To better protect your heart and kidneys. Atorvastatin lowers cholesterol, and higher-dose lisinopril helps your heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making great progress. PT says you can transfer using your right foot. No weight on the left side yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long before I can walk with a prosthesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes weeks to months. First, the wound must fully heal. Then rehab will train you gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge tomorrow. You’ll go to a rehab facility for continued care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, increased redness, drainage, or new pain. Keep the site elevated and don’t soak it in water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your diabetic, low-fat diet. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain over 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’ll go to ___ rehab facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Continue vancomycin and ceftazidime with dialysis for two weeks. Follow up with vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the apixaban?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, apixaban twice daily. No driving until your surgeon clears you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow all the instructions. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rehab will help you adjust. We’re here if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I stop smoking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, strongly. Smoking narrows blood vessels and harms circulation, especially important now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. My PCP can help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they can provide support and resources. It’s one of the best things you can do for healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need help at home after rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re wheelchair-dependent now. Services will be arranged based on your progress in rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye? I can’t see out of the right one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your retinopathy has caused blindness in that eye. Continue seeing your eye doctor regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. Managing your diabetes, heart, and wounds carefully will help keep you healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve been through a lot, and you’re handling it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call your doctor if anything changes. Safe travels to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a summary to your PCP so they can help manage your pain meds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I don’t want to be in pain or confused about my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having some trouble with urination and a feeling of fullness in your lower belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I’ve had this pressure for weeks, even after finishing antibiotics for a UTI. And now I’m leaking urine without warning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned no burning or blood, which is good. But your urine test shows a lot of white blood cells and bacteria, and your white count is high. This suggests another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I just finished gentamicin last week. Is it the same kind of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet, but given your history with resistant bacteria, we’re starting you on meropenem, a strong IV antibiotic, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had Klebsiella before. Is it that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We sent a urine culture, and if it’s Klebsiella, meropenem works well against it. We’ll know more in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about getting the IV meds at dialysis. Last time they didn’t have the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working with your dialysis center. Meropenem will be given after your HD sessions. We’re confirming they can provide it for your full 14-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if they can’t? I don’t want to stay here longer than necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s an oral option—fosfomycin—if the bacteria is sensitive to it. We’ve requested that test. Results should be back soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. I’d prefer a pill if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll let you know as soon as we get the sensitivity results. In the meantime, we also noticed your bladder is very full on exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can’t empty it. I’ve been struggling since the last UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re retaining urine. We’re restarting straight catheterizations daily to help empty your bladder and prevent more infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember doing that before. Who will help me at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for a nurse to come daily to perform the catheterization. It’s important to keep doing this regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it. But I really want to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your response. Your sodium is low, around 130, which is typical for you. We’re keeping fluids limited to 1 liter per day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’ve had that for years. Is it related to the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly. It’s likely due to fluid overload from kidney disease. We’re managing it with your dialysis and fluid restriction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an ultrasound of your kidneys and bladder. No abscess, which is good. But your bladder is very full and has some thickening and debris.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why the catheterizations are so important. The ultrasound also showed small kidney stones, but they’re not blocking anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Nothing to do about them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They’re small and not causing issues. We’ll keep an eye on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—from 13 to 9.6. That means the antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the fosfomycin sensitivity. If it’s sensitive, you might switch to an oral antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But if not, I’ll need the IV meropenem at dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We tried calling your dialysis center, but they’re still checking if they can give it on your next session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to wait. I’ll go to the ED if I can’t get it. Or maybe that pheresis unit can help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We called them, but they were closed. We can’t confirm availability. It’s risky to leave without a clear plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I need to go home. I’ll follow up with my PCP tomorrow to check the sensitivity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If fosfomycin doesn’t work, and meropenem isn’t available at dialysis, you may need to go to the ED for a dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do what I have to. I just want to avoid another long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We still don’t have the fosfomycin result, but your dialysis center says they’ll have meropenem available soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home? I’ll get the IV med at dialysis or follow up with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll continue meropenem with dialysis for 14 days. And keep daily catheterizations. Call your PCP to check the culture result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure I get the treatment, one way or another.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your records to your PCP. If you develop fever, pain, or can’t get the antibiotic, go to the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been through this before. I know when to seek help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just stay on top of the antibiotics and catheterizations. We’re discharging you with home health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some body twitching for the past day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started yesterday. My arms and legs keep jerking. It feels like when I took gabapentin before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you were restarted on gabapentin recently. Can you tell me why it was restarted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My neuropathy pain has been bad, so my doctor thought it might help. But this twitching is just like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Given your kidney disease, gabapentin can build up and cause these kinds of symptoms. We’ll stop it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s not something more serious? I was worried it was a seizure or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. You’re alert, your exam is stable, and no new weakness. The twitching without confusion or loss of consciousness points more to medication side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I also had jelly beans before it started—could that have triggered it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The jelly beans likely caused a blood sugar spike—we saw it was 221 this morning. High sugars can worsen neuropathy symptoms, but the twitching is most likely from gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll avoid sweets too. What about my dialysis? I’m due today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for hemodialysis at noon. That will help clear the gabapentin from your system and should improve the twitching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my urine test showed bacteria—do I need antibiotics again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have bacteria in your urine, but you’re not having fever, pain, or urgency. Since you just finished a course for Klebsiella, we won’t restart antibiotics unless symptoms develop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t want another long hospital stay like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The twitching is much better. I haven’t had any jerks since I woke up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The dialysis helped clear the medication. We’ll keep gabapentin stopped permanently due to your kidney condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. What should I do if the nerve pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with your primary doctor to find a safer option. For now, your other medications are unchanged, including insulin and heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable, and you’ve done well overnight. We’re clearing you to go home with home health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. So just no more gabapentin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And follow up with your doctor in a few days. Call if twitching returns or if you develop fever, swelling, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep weighing myself every morning like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing a great job managing your health. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re here today for a planned surgery to create a new dialysis access in your left arm, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been on dialysis through the catheter in my neck, but they said it’s better to have a graft in my arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re going to place a loop graft in your left arm so you can have more reliable and safer long-term dialysis access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard they might use a synthetic tube. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we used a PTFE graft because your vessels have some calcification. It’s a strong, safe material that works well for patients like you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m a little worried about my hand going numb or cold after this. I’ve had circulation issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We checked during surgery, and there’s a good pulse in your wrist. Your hand is a bit cooler than the other side, but that’s expected and close to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the numbness in my fingertips? That’s been there a while, but I don’t want it to get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned mild numbness, which we believe is related to your diabetic neuropathy. We didn’t see any new nerve issues from the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s your left arm feeling? Any pain, coldness, or blue fingers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain, no blue fingers. It’s still a little cool, and the tips of my fingers are numb like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re watching closely for any signs of poor blood flow. The graft has a strong thrill and bruit, which means it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session through the neck catheter. Everything went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So now what? Is the new graft ready to use?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. It needs about 2–3 weeks to mature before we can use it for dialysis. You’ll keep using your neck catheter until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. Your graft is patent, and your hand exam remains stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home? I don’t want to miss anything serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the access clinic immediately if you have fevers, pain, coldness, or blue fingers in the left hand. Also check daily for the thrill—the buzzing feeling over the graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I don’t feel the buzz?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could mean the graft is blocked. Call right away—don’t wait for your next dialysis. Also, no blood pressures or needle sticks in that arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No heavy lifting either, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep it under 10 pounds, and avoid tight clothes or jewelry on that side. Elevate your arm to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. You’ll continue all your regular medications, including insulin and apixaban.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have tramadol for mild pain and now also hydrocodone for breakthrough pain—take only as needed. And we added docusate for constipation prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Keep your follow-up with the access team, and continue dialysis as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home with services. Take care, and call if anything changes with your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in because of diarrhea and redness in your left arm. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad diarrhea for two days. But before that, I hadn’t had a bowel movement in days. And my left arm—since the surgery—it’s been swollen, and now it’s red and sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You had that AV graft placed in your left arm about a week ago, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was on Dilaudid for pain, and then I couldn’t go to the bathroom. Then suddenly, I started having accidents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like overflow diarrhea—when stool builds up and leaks around the blockage. We’ll check with an X-ray. Your arm is red and tender—any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But the redness worries me. Is the graft infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about cellulitis—skin infection near the graft. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin to treat it. We’ll monitor your labs and symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just tired. Can I rest now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll check on you regularly. Let the nurse know if you feel worse or have pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show a slightly high white blood cell count, which supports infection. But no fever, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still red and swollen, but no pus. We’ll keep the antibiotics going. Also, your kidney function is stable, but we’ll adjust meds accordingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I missed dialysis yesterday. When can I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled hemodialysis for today at noon. You’ll have another session tomorrow before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my blood sugar? I didn’t take my evening insulin last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sugars have been between 100 and 200. We’re keeping you on your usual NPH and rapid-acting insulin. It’s okay you skipped the small dose—just continue as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but okay. Any news on the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray showed a lot of stool in your colon—no blockage. The diarrhea is likely from constipation caused by the pain medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not sick from the infection in my gut?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The C. diff test was negative. We’re starting a bowel regimen—senna and docusate—to prevent this from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t take Dilaudid again. It messed everything up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain with acetaminophen instead. Opioids can really slow your gut, especially with your diabetes and gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is coming down—7.4 from 10.2. That means the infection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Less tender today. Still some redness and swelling, but it’s getting better. We’ll switch you to oral doxycycline to finish the antibiotic course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doxycycline is safe. Just take it with a full glass of water and sit upright for 30 minutes to avoid stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the graft? Is it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant surgeon saw you. There’s concern about blood flow—possible ‘steal syndrome’—where the graft pulls blood away from your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I lose my hand?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. But you’ll need to see the transplant clinic next week. They may consider closing the graft if it’s causing problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on all your home meds—apixaban, lisinopril, atorvastatin, insulin, and the rest. We adjusted metoprolol due to your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your second dialysis session. Your labs are looking better—creatinine down to 1.8, potassium normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had a few loose stools today, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected as your bowels clear out. Keep taking the stool softener and fiber. Avoid opioids unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll finish the doxycycline at home for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—transplant surgery for your graft, primary care for diabetes and dialysis, and we’ve given you a prescription for ivermectin in case of scabies exposure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have scabies, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs today, but you were exposed during your last stay. The ivermectin is preventive—just one dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I should watch my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Weigh yourself every morning. Call if you gain more than three pounds in a day—could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no blood pressure or blood draws on my left arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Protect the graft. Use your right arm for all procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over your meds before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check. Your arm is less red, you’re afebrile, and your labs are stable. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if the arm gets worse, or if you have fever, trouble breathing, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge. Someone will help you to the car.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: blood cultures came back negative—no bloodstream infection. All clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take it easy, follow your instructions, and we’ll see how you do at your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’re discharging you now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you were brought in after feeling shaky and clammy during rehab. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was with my therapist yesterday and suddenly felt weak, dizzy, and very sweaty. I vomited a few times the night before. My blood sugar was high, they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your records. You were found to have very high blood sugar—983—and an acid buildup in your blood, which is diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I’ve had DKA before. Did that cause my heart issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. You also had a heart enzyme called troponin that was very high, which means there was heart muscle injury—what we call a non-ST elevation MI, or NSTEMI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t have chest pain. Is that possible?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with diabetes and nerve damage, heart attacks can happen without pain. We’re concerned the DKA may have triggered the heart event, or vice versa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. What about my heart function?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last echo showed good function, but now we see your ejection fraction is down to about 19%. That means your heart isn’t pumping as well as it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this is new? What caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to blockages in your heart arteries. We’ll do a stress test and possibly a cardiac catheterization to find out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your troponin levels peaked and are now coming down. That’s a good sign the heart injury isn’t ongoing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your DKA has resolved. The insulin drip was stopped, and we’ve restarted your NPH insulin. We adjusted the dose to 30 units in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll make sure to take it. What about that finger issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have redness and swelling at the base of your right index finger. Hand surgery thinks it’s cellulitis from a chronic paronychia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Should I be worried about the bone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got an X-ray. No signs of bone infection. You’ll start IV antibiotics and do warm soaks. We’ll switch to oral antibiotics later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stress test showed severe fixed defects in the front and side walls of your heart. That means those areas have poor blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I need a stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend cardiac catheterization to place stents in the blocked arteries. We’ll do it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it help my heart function improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Restoring blood flow may help your heart recover some strength over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed dialysis earlier. We removed 2.8 liters of fluid. Your lungs are clearer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less bloated. Is that why I had the crackles in my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluid buildup from heart and kidney issues. Dialysis helps manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray of your finger shows no bone infection. The redness is improving with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I stop the IV meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to oral doxycycline tomorrow. You’ll take it for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the cath lab. They found severe blockages and placed stents in three areas of your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did everything go okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the procedure was successful. But they noticed a small connection between an artery and vein in your right groin—an AV fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and not causing any problems. Vascular surgery says to monitor it, no treatment needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. What about my blood thinners?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on aspirin and a new pill called clopidogrel. They help prevent clots after stents. Your apixaban dose was lowered to 2.5 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your kidney disease and the new blood thinners, we lowered it to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound confirmed the AV fistula is small and likely not new. It’s not affecting your circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just monitoring. Your finger is healing well, and your heart enzymes are trending down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. You’ll need to follow up with cardiology, endocrinology, and continue dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? Should I adjust it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on 30 units NPH in the morning. Check your sugars regularly. The endocrine team will see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Continue doxycycline for your finger, and take all your heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds, have shortness of breath, chest pain, or finger redness worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the AV fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No action needed. Just keep your follow-up with cardiology to monitor your heart function and stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll follow everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ , one of the surgical team. You were admitted because of ongoing pain and circulation issues in your left hand related to your dialysis access graft. Do you remember discussing this with your surgeon before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had that graft placed a while back. It caused hand pain—like coldness, numbness. I was told it might be stealing blood flow. But I didn’t want it removed at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. That’s called ‘steal syndrome.’ Your symptoms didn’t get worse, so you kept using it for dialysis. But now there are new ulcers on your left hand, and your right hand is also having circulation problems. We think it’s safer to remove the graft now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re going to take it out? But how will I get dialysis then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do the graft removal today. After that, a temporary dialysis catheter will be placed in your neck so you can continue dialysis safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m nervous about the surgery. Is it risky with my heart and diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history—your heart function is stable, and your blood work is within acceptable limits. The surgery is relatively straightforward. We’ll monitor you closely. Your blood pressure and blood sugar will be checked often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my hand—will it get better after the graft is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Removing the graft should improve blood flow to your hand. But we also saw that your arteries are quite calcified, which makes circulation difficult. We’ll get a CT scan today to see exactly what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many scans. Will this one show why my fingers keep cracking and forming scabs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT will show the blood vessels in your arms and hands. If there’s poor flow due to blockages, that could explain the ulcers and fissures. We may need to see a hand surgeon later for possible revascularization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Revascularization? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means trying to restore blood flow through surgery or a procedure, like opening up narrowed arteries. But we’ll know more after the scan. For now, focus on getting through today’s surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The surgery went well. We successfully ligated the graft in your left arm. You tolerated it without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My arm feels heavy, but no sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There might be some swelling or bruising. We saw a small hematoma under the dressing, but it’s not concerning. You’ll have a new dialysis line placed tomorrow morning so you can dialyze safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why not today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We wanted to make sure you were stable after surgery. The procedure to place the line requires imaging guidance and a radiology team, which is scheduled for tomorrow at 12 p.m.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the CT scan—did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The larger arteries up to your elbow are open, but the smaller ones in your forearms and hands are heavily calcified. We can’t tell if blood is flowing through them on this type of scan. The hand surgeon reviewed it and thinks you might benefit from a more detailed test later—maybe an MRA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my hands won’t heal unless they fix the blood flow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s part of it. Your diabetes and kidney disease also slow healing. But improving circulation could help prevent more ulcers. The hand surgeon will see you as an outpatient to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already lost part of my leg. I don’t want to lose fingers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re acting now. The graft was likely making things worse. Removing it was the right step. We’ll do everything we can to preserve your hand function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’ll place your dialysis catheter in the left side of your neck. It’ll go into the jugular vein and reach your heart. You’ll be given some sedation, and the radiologist will use ultrasound and X-ray to guide it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll feel some pressure and numbing shots, but the sedation will help you relax. Most patients tolerate it well. Afterward, you’ll get dialysis through it, and we’ll make sure it’s working before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your dialysis catheter was placed successfully. The tip is in the right atrium, and both ports are flowing well. You just finished your dialysis session and did fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. Just sleepy. Is the catheter permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This one is temporary. Since your left arm graft is gone, your team will decide if you need a new access—maybe in your right arm or leg. That’ll be discussed at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if everything stays stable. Your hand pain is no worse, you’re eating, and you’ve done dialysis safely through the new line. We’ll send you home with instructions and a follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop fever, redness or pus at the incision or catheter site, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if your hand pain worsens. Also, monitor your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual medicines—insulin, blood pressure pills, aspirin, apixaban, and the others. We’ve sent the updated list to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take tramadol for pain. Is that okay with the other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but take it only as needed. Avoid driving while on it. And don’t take extra acetaminophen—stick to the prescribed dose to protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hand surgeon appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for next week. They’ll evaluate whether you’re a candidate for a procedure to improve blood flow to your hands. It’s important to keep that visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. A nurse will go over wound care and how to keep the catheter site clean. You’re doing well—just keep following up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your CT also showed gallstones and a small cyst in your pancreas. Nothing urgent, but your primary doctor should follow up on those with an MRI later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More tests? I’m tired of being poked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But this is just monitoring. The cyst is likely benign, but we want to make sure it doesn’t change. Your doctor will coordinate it when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. As long as it’s not surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery planned. Focus on healing your hands and staying on track with dialysis and diabetes care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your wheelchair ready shortly, and a nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having these shaking episodes—started a couple days ago. My head started nodding, then my whole body was trembling. It finally stopped last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, confusion, or weakness during the tremors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or weakness. Just the shaking. I’ve had something like this before when I started gabapentin, but I haven’t taken that in months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. And you mentioned finger pain—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my right index finger has been black and numb for a while. It’s gotten more swollen and tender lately. I think it’s from poor circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see in your history you’ve had vascular issues and a dialysis graft closed recently. We’ll examine your finger and get some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected? Shouldn’t I be on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, there’s no pus or spreading redness, so we don’t think it’s actively infected. We’ll hold off on antibiotics unless things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tremors? I was really scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs and did a CT scan of your head. No stroke or bleed. Neurology thinks the tremors were likely due to metabolic changes from your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So dialysis might help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re scheduled for dialysis tonight. That should help stabilize your electrolytes and may have prevented the tremors from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. But what about my finger? It hurts more every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted plastic surgery. They agree the tissue is dead and may need to be removed, but it’s not an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Removed? You mean amputation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, possibly just the tip. But first, we’d need an angiogram to check blood flow. You declined that for now, so we’ll manage the pain and plan follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just worried about more surgeries. I’ve been through so much already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand completely. That’s why we’re not pushing anything now. The priority is keeping you stable and comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I do have chills sometimes, though not now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve seen that in your chart. They’ve been intermittent, not linked to fever or infection. Likely related to your autonomic neuropathy from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. My diabetes has caused so many problems—eyes, feet, now hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re managing all of that. Your insulin, blood pressure, and heart medications are all continuing as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want anything changed without talking to me first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll always discuss changes with you. Now, your labs show mild hyponatremia, but it’s stable and likely from fluid retention due to kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that cause problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Dialysis will help correct it. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel better knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more clear-headed. No tremors since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs after dialysis are stable. The tremors haven’t returned, which supports the idea they were metabolic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I probably won’t have them again if I keep up with dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the expectation. Staying on schedule with dialysis should help prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about my finger? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still the same—dry gangrene, no signs of infection. Plastic surgery will see you in clinic in two weeks to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll need that angiogram before any surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to see if there’s any chance to improve blood flow. But it’s outpatient—we’ll schedule it when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ve been stable, no tremors, and your finger hasn’t worsened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop fever, chills, redness spreading on your finger, or any new weakness, speech changes, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tremors—if they come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if they don’t stop. But keep up with dialysis, and they’re unlikely to return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my follow-up with the surgeon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks. They’ll guide you on the next steps for your finger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your time and explanations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll make sure you have all your medications and instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on tramadol for pain—can I keep using that as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, up to twice a day. And acetaminophen every 8 hours if needed. Just avoid NSAIDs—they’re not safe with your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No ibuprofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than three pounds in a day—could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I’ve had heart failure before, so I know to watch for swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. You’re well-informed. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll go home with a nurse today. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think you’ve covered everything. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.
