conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will be in shortly to assist you with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling sick since your dialysis yesterday. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had nausea and vomiting since I left dialysis. It’s been really bad the last 24 hours. I also have stomach pain and my hand has been hurting more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I’ve felt a little chilly. And I haven’t had a bowel movement in five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ve done some tests. Your white blood cell count is high, which suggests infection. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? Where?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it might be at your recent finger amputation site. There’s redness and swelling, and your pain is worse. We’re calling it cellulitis—skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. But I didn’t think it was infected. It’s just been painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain could be from both infection and poor blood flow. We’re starting antibiotics through your IV to treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my stomach? I’ve been nauseous for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT showed a large mass of stool in your rectum—about 8 cm. That’s likely causing the nausea and pain. We’ll start treatment to help you pass it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had constipation for years because of my diabetes. But this feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gastroparesis from diabetes slows your stomach, and now the backed-up stool is adding to it. We’ll give you fluids and a laxative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The CT also mentioned something about a metal object?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a 1.4 cm metal piece near your cecum, in the fat tissue. It’s new since your last scan. We’re not sure what it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never had surgery there. I didn’t swallow anything metal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be from an old appendectomy you don’t remember, or something else. It’s not causing a blockage. But we recommend an outpatient colonoscopy to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stay in the hospital for that. I need to get home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. You can have the colonoscopy later as an outpatient. We’ll arrange it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my blood sugar has been high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 393 today. Infection can spike blood sugar. We’ve adjusted your insulin—now 30 units NPH in the morning and 5 at night, plus Humalog with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 35 in the morning. Is this safer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to avoid high sugars in the morning. We’ll monitor it. No ketones, so no DKA, but we need better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea is a bit better today, I hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I kept breakfast down. Did the laxative help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You passed some stool, and your belly is less firm. The big mass is breaking down. We’ll keep the Miralax going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the infection? Is the antibiotic working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is still high but stable. We’re continuing vancomycin and ceftazidime, given during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hand pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still likely due to poor blood flow from your vascular disease. We discussed angiography, but you declined?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I know the risk, but I don’t want more procedures. I understand I might lose more of my hand if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll manage pain with Dilaudid and keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows improvement in mild fluid buildup. Your lungs are clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been breathing easier. Is my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart is enlarged, which we knew, but no new issues. Your troponin was slightly elevated, but likely due to your kidney disease, not a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back positive for yeast. We’ll start oral fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. People with diabetes and catheters can get yeast. It’s treatable. We’ll give you a single dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Nausea is gone, you’re eating, and your hand infection is improving. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get vancomycin and ceftazidime during your dialysis sessions for 10 days total. The clinic will give them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. Try to use it sparingly. We’ll reassess at your hand follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the colonoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it as an outpatient. It’s important to rule out any issue with that metal fragment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do it. Just not now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your vitals are stable, you’re eating well, and your infection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your antibiotics during dialysis, use Miralax daily, monitor blood sugar, and take Dilaudid only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor, hand surgeon, and we’ll set up the colonoscopy. Call us if fever, vomiting, or hand redness worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.
